standard.title: Media influence on identity and diversity
standard.description: the influence of a range of media, including social media, in shaping identity and attitudes to diversity
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined different experiences of and debates about Australia's national identity and citizenship including perspectives of First Nations Australians and migrant groups (AC9HC8K06). They understand identity as shaped by culture and community but have not yet examined how media actively constructs and circulates representations that shape identity and attitudes.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how media, including social media, influences the shaping of identity and attitudes to diversity, and analyse media representations of different groups in Australian society.

nodes.label: How media constructs representations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how media construct representations of groups and why these representations matter for community attitudes.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain that media do not simply report reality but make choices about how to represent groups, and identify at least one example of a media representation of a specific group.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how media represent different groups in Australian society — including First Nations Australians, immigrant groups, male and female sporting figures, and people with disability; explain how these representations are constructed through selection, framing and emphasis; identify the impact those representations can have on community attitudes.
wider: Compare how the same group (e.g. a refugee community, First Nations Australians) is represented across different media outlets and evaluate what drives the differences
Trace how representations of a specific group have changed over time and assess what has driven that change
Examine representations in advertising or entertainment media and assess how they shape or challenge stereotypes about gender, ethnicity or disability
nodes.hinge_reason: If students treat media representations as neutral descriptions rather than constructed artefacts, they cannot undertake the social media analysis in Node 2, which depends on understanding media choices as active shaping forces rather than mirrors of community attitudes.

response_modes.reason: Students need explicit scaffolding on the distinction between representation and reality — that the same event or community can be represented in multiple ways, and that choices about framing carry consequences. A comparative analysis exercise (same event, two different outlets) makes this concrete.

success_criteria: Explains that media representations involve active choices about framing and selection
Identifies a specific example of media representation of a group and explains how it shapes community attitudes

nodes.label: Social media, identity and human rights campaigns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how social media influences identity formation and explain how human rights campaigns use social media to engage the public.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one way social media influences identity and one way it has been used in a human rights campaign.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate how social media shapes identity (including the construction of personal and group identity online) and attitudes to diversity; investigate a human rights campaign that uses social media and how members of the public have engaged with the issue; assess both the reach and the limitations of social media as a tool for civic engagement.
wider: Analyse a specific social media campaign on a human rights or diversity issue (e.g. #BlackLivesMatter, #MeToo, LGBTIQ+ campaigns) and evaluate its impact on public attitudes and policy
Investigate how algorithms shape what content people see and how this can create filter bubbles that reinforce existing identity and attitudes
Examine how social media platforms are used by both those advocating for diversity and those spreading divisive or hateful content, and evaluate what responsibilities platforms have

response_modes.reason: Social media's role in identity is experienced differently by students in different communities. Using both a national-scale campaign and a local or youth-focused example makes the analysis personally anchored and more critical.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Social media and identity is a domain students have direct experience with, creating unusually rich conditions for analysis. Advancing students can examine algorithmic influence, the performativity of online identity, and the dual use of platforms — topics that extend the analysis significantly while remaining within Year 9 scope.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one way social media influences identity or attitudes to diversity
Describes a human rights campaign that used social media and explains how it sought to engage public participation
